questions.question: What is a build tool and why do Java projects need one?
questions.title: What Is a Build Tool?
questions.direct_answer: A build tool coordinates tasks such as compiling source, running tests, resolving declared dependencies, and packaging artifacts. It makes the build process repeatable and automatable across developer and CI machines. Identical build files alone do not guarantee byte-for-byte reproducibility; toolchains, repository contents, environment inputs, and reproducible-build settings also matter.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands compilation, testing, dependency resolution, packaging, and repeatability as separate build responsibilities.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing a build tool only as a dependency downloader or claiming one build file guarantees identical bytes everywhere.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use one concrete Maven or Gradle command and explain which configured lifecycle or tasks it runs.

sections.title: Why Build Tools Exist
sections.content:
A **build tool** turns a project's declared build rules into repeatable actions. In a Java project it can compile source, run tests, resolve dependencies, copy resources, generate reports, and package a JAR or WAR. Plugins add tasks such as code generation, coverage, or container-image creation.

For example, `mvn verify` reads the POM, resolves required plugins and libraries, compiles the configured sources, runs the tests bound to the lifecycle, and performs checks configured before `verify`. Gradle performs the comparable work through a task graph. The exact actions still come from the project configuration and plugins; a build tool does not run every possible check automatically.

Automation improves consistency, but the build file alone does not guarantee identical bytes on every machine. A reproducible build also controls the JDK and tool versions, dependencies and repositories, environment-dependent inputs, timestamps, and plugin behavior.

sections.title: What a Build Tool Actually Does
sections.content:
amber|Source|~Java and resources|declared project inputs|compiler configuration|generated sources when configured
blue|Build actions|~Compile and test|plugin goals or tasks|checks and reports|failures stop the pipeline
emerald|Dependencies|~Resolve coordinates|local and remote repositories|transitive graph|scope and conflict rules
violet|Artifact|~JAR, WAR, or other output|repeatable process|publish only when configured|reproducibility needs controlled inputs

sections.title: Build Tool Configuration Example (Maven pom.xml)
sections.content:
```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    
    <groupId>com.company</groupId>
    <artifactId>order-service</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
    
    <dependencies>
        <!-- Build tool downloads this automatically -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
            <version>3.2.0</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
    
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <!-- Automates packaging as executable JAR -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
```

sections.title: When Build Tools Are Essential
sections.content: Use a build tool from day one on any Java project. **For team projects**, it eliminates the "works on my machine" problem by standardizing how dependencies are resolved and code is compiled. **For microservices**, where you might have 15 services each with different dependencies, build tools prevent version conflicts and manage transitive dependencies automatically. **For CI/CD pipelines**, tools like Jenkins and GitHub Actions run Maven or Gradle commands to ensure automated testing and deployment. Even a single-file learning project benefits because you avoid manually downloading Spring Boot JARs and setting classpaths.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking build tools only download libraries**: Freshers often say "Maven downloads JARs" but miss that it also compiles code, runs tests, generates documentation, and orchestrates the entire build lifecycle.
- **Not understanding the local cache**: They don't realize dependencies download once to ~/.m2/repository and are reused across projects, so they delete it thinking it's temporary storage.
- **Ignoring build reproducibility**: They commit dependency JARs to Git instead of declaring and managing versions through the build configuration and any chosen locking or verification mechanism, causing version drift across team members.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Automates the build:** compilation, tests, resources, checks, and packaging.
- **Resolves declared dependencies:** including permitted transitive dependencies.
- **Uses plugins or tasks:** the configuration decides what actually runs.
- **Supports repeatability:** developers and CI can invoke the same process.
- **Reproducibility needs all inputs controlled:** not only the POM or build script.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A build tool automates the steps needed to turn source code into a tested, packaged artifact. In Java that normally includes compiling classes, resolving declared libraries, running tests, copying resources, and creating a JAR or WAR. Maven expresses this through a POM, lifecycle phases, and plugin goals; Gradle uses a task graph and build DSL.

For example, running `mvn verify` on a configured service executes the earlier default-lifecycle phases and any checks bound through `verify`. If a test fails, the build can stop before publishing an artifact. This gives developers and CI one documented process instead of separate manual `javac`, classpath, and packaging commands. It supports reproducible work, but byte-for-byte reproducibility still depends on controlling the JDK, plugins, repository content, environment, and generated timestamps.

questions.question: What is the difference between a JAR and a WAR file?
questions.title: JAR vs WAR Files
questions.direct_answer: A JAR is a general Java archive for classes and resources; it can be a library or an executable application. A WAR follows the web-application archive layout for deployment to a servlet container. Spring Boot can build executable JARs or WARs with nested runtime dependencies, but an embedded servlet server appears only in web applications that include one.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can separate archive layout, executable packaging, and the servlet-container deployment model.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying every JAR contains an embedded server or every WAR requires `web.xml`.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Spring Boot can repackage both formats and that the server exists only for a web application that includes one.

sections.title: Java Packaging Formats
sections.content:
Both formats use ZIP-based Java archive conventions, but they serve different deployment contracts. A **JAR** is the general archive for Java classes and resources. It may be a library, an ordinary application archive, or an executable archive when its manifest and contents support launching.

A **WAR** follows the Jakarta Servlet web-application layout. Application classes and libraries normally appear under `WEB-INF/classes` and `WEB-INF/lib`, and the archive can be deployed to a compatible servlet container. `web.xml` is optional for applications that use annotations or programmatic configuration.

Spring Boot can repackage a JAR or WAR with nested runtime dependencies and its launcher. A servlet web application can include an embedded server for standalone launching. A non-web Boot application does not gain a server merely because it is packaged as a Boot archive.

sections.title: JAR vs WAR at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|JAR|~Java Archive|classes + libs + manifest|Spring Boot executable Boot archive|run with java -jar
blue|WAR|~Web App Archive|WEB-INF structure|servlets and JSPs|deploy to Tomcat/JBoss
emerald|Modern default|~Embedded server|self-contained|cloud and Docker friendly|one artifact to ship
violet|When WAR fits|~Shared container|legacy app servers|central ops control|compliance mandates

sections.title: JAR vs WAR: Build and Run Commands
sections.content:
```bash
# JAR (Spring Boot, embedded Tomcat) — runs itself
mvn package
java -jar target/order-service-1.0.0.jar

# WAR (deploy to an external servlet container)
# pom.xml:  <packaging>war</packaging>
mvn package                       # produces target/order-service-1.0.0.war
cp target/order-service-1.0.0.war $TOMCAT_HOME/webapps/   # external Tomcat hosts it
```

sections.title: JAR vs WAR Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | JAR | WAR |
|---|---|---|
| Main role | General Java archive | Servlet web-application archive |
| Required layout | Java archive conventions and manifest as needed | `WEB-INF/classes`, `WEB-INF/lib`, and web resources |
| Direct launch | Only when packaged with a suitable entry point/runtime | Possible for an executable Boot WAR; ordinary WARs are container deployments |
| Typical use | Libraries, command-line apps, services | Applications for external servlet containers |
| Descriptor | Manifest may name an entry point | `web.xml` is optional in modern servlet applications |

sections.title: When to Use Each Format
sections.content: Use a JAR for libraries and for applications designed to run as their own process. A Spring Boot web JAR commonly contains nested dependencies and a server implementation, but a plain library JAR does not. Use a WAR when the deployment contract is an external compatible servlet container or application server. A Boot WAR may also be executable when configured that way. Choose from the target runtime and operations model, not from a rule that all modern systems must use one format.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying every JAR is executable:** a library JAR usually has no application entry point.
- **Saying every executable JAR embeds Tomcat:** non-web apps have no web server, and web apps can use another supported server.
- **Treating `web.xml` as mandatory:** modern servlet applications may use annotations or programmatic configuration.
- **Saying a WAR can never run directly:** Spring Boot can create an executable WAR while retaining WAR layout.
- **Deploying a Boot JAR as a WAR:** select the packaging and dependency setup for the actual target container.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **JAR:** general archive for Java classes and resources; may be a library or application.
- **WAR:** servlet web-application layout for a compatible container.
- **`WEB-INF`:** holds web-app classes and libraries; `web.xml` is not always required.
- **Spring Boot:** can create executable JARs and WARs with nested dependencies.
- **Embedded server:** depends on the web application dependencies and packaging setup, not the `.jar` suffix alone.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A JAR is the general Java archive format. It can contain a library or application classes and resources, and it is directly launchable only when it has the required entry information and runtime contents. A WAR is a web-application archive with the servlet layout, including `WEB-INF/classes` and `WEB-INF/lib`, intended for a compatible servlet container. Modern WARs do not always need `web.xml`.

For example, a Spring Boot REST service is commonly repackaged as an executable JAR with its runtime dependencies and a servlet server dependency, then run with `java -jar`. A company that deploys applications into an existing external servlet container may package the same kind of app as a WAR and mark the external container dependency appropriately. Spring Boot can also make an executable WAR, so the important distinction is archive layout and deployment model rather than 'JAR always runs itself, WAR never does.'

questions.question: What is the history of Java build tools — Ant, Maven, and Gradle?
questions.title: Ant vs Maven vs Gradle: A Brief History
questions.direct_answer: Ant (early 2000s) uses explicit XML targets and leaves project structure mostly to the build author. Maven 1 appeared in the early 2000s and Maven 2 in 2005, introducing the POM, repository dependency model, standard lifecycles, and conventions. Gradle began in 2008 and reached 1.0 in 2012, combining a task graph with Groovy and later Kotlin DSLs, up-to-date checks, and build caching.

interviewer_intent.testing: Breadth of knowledge and awareness of the evolution of tooling — shows the candidate reads beyond tutorials
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing Maven and Gradle exist without understanding why each tool was created or what problems they solved
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Ant with Ivy added dependency management but never achieved Maven's ecosystem dominance due to lack of standardization

sections.title: Evolution of Java Build Automation
sections.content:
Java build tools developed toward more shared convention and reusable dependency resolution. **Ant**, released around 2000, gives build authors XML targets made from explicit tasks. It is flexible, but each project defines much of its own lifecycle and layout; Ivy can add dependency resolution.

The **Maven** project began in the early 2000s, and Maven 2 arrived in 2005 with the POM model, standard lifecycles, repository coordinates, transitive dependency resolution, and strong directory conventions. A Maven build can still be customized through plugins, but ordinary projects share a familiar shape.

**Gradle** began in 2008 and reached version 1.0 in 2012. It models work as a task graph configured with Groovy or Kotlin DSLs and supports up-to-date checks and build caching. These tools overlap today; the best choice depends on an existing build, team knowledge, ecosystem, required customization, and measured build behavior.

sections.title: Three Generations of Java Build Tools
sections.content:
amber|Ant|~Explicit targets and tasks|XML build file|layout chosen by project|Ivy can add dependencies
blue|Maven|~Model and lifecycle|POM and coordinates|strong standard conventions|plugin-bound phases
emerald|Gradle|~Task graph and DSL|Groovy or Kotlin|up-to-date checks|local or remote build cache
violet|Choice today|~Respect existing build|team skills|ecosystem and customization|measure real build behavior

sections.title: Build Tool Evolution in Code
sections.content:
```xml
<!-- Ant: the target lists the tasks explicitly -->
<target name="compile">
  <mkdir dir="build/classes"/>
  <javac srcdir="src" destdir="build/classes"/>
</target>
```

```xml
<!-- Maven: packaging and plugins bind goals to standard phases -->
<project>
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  <groupId>example</groupId><artifactId>app</artifactId><version>1.0</version>
</project>
```

```kotlin
// Gradle: plugins contribute tasks to a configurable task graph
plugins { java }
repositories { mavenCentral() }
```

sections.title: When Each Tool Makes Sense
sections.content:
Use **Maven** for enterprise Spring Boot projects where stability and IDE integration matter. Most companies have existing Maven infrastructure and Nexus repositories, so Maven is the path of least resistance.

Use **Gradle** when you need build flexibility — multi-language projects (Java plus Kotlin), Android apps, or custom build logic like generating code from OpenAPI specs. Gradle's build cache and incremental compilation shine on large codebases. **Ant** is legacy maintenance only — if you inherit an Ant project, consider migrating to Maven or Gradle unless there's complex custom build logic that's too risky to rewrite. Maven or Gradle is normally a clearer greenfield default, while project constraints can still justify another tool.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not understanding why Maven replaced Ant**: Freshers think it's just fashion, but Maven's Central Repository and standardized lifecycle solved real coordination problems in large teams.
- **Assuming Gradle is always better**: They pick Gradle for a simple Spring Boot CRUD app where Maven would be simpler and more familiar to most teams.
- **Forgetting about Ant with Ivy**: They don't realize Ivy tried to add dependency management to Ant, but It did not give Ant one universal project lifecycle because every project configured it differently — there was no standard like Maven's pom.xml.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Ant:** explicit XML targets and tasks; project conventions are mostly author-defined.
- **Ivy:** can add repository dependency resolution to Ant builds.
- **Maven:** POM, standard lifecycle/layout, repository coordinates, and transitive dependencies.
- **Gradle:** task graph, Groovy/Kotlin DSL, up-to-date checks, and build cache.
- **Timeline:** Ant around 2000; Maven project early 2000s/Maven 2 in 2005; Gradle began 2008/1.0 in 2012.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Ant, Maven, and Gradle reflect different build models rather than a simple sequence where each completely replaced the previous tool. Ant uses XML targets made from explicit tasks, so the build author controls the steps and project layout. Ivy can add dependency resolution. Maven adds a POM, repository coordinates, a standard lifecycle, and strong conventions such as `src/main/java`, which gives unrelated projects a familiar structure.

Gradle began in 2008 and released 1.0 in 2012. It uses a programmable Groovy or Kotlin DSL around a task graph and supports features such as up-to-date checks and build caching. For example, an existing Ant build may remain sensible when it contains stable custom tasks, while a conventional Java service may fit Maven and a highly customized multi-project or Android build may fit Gradle. I would choose from project needs and team ownership, not from a universal speed ranking.

questions.question: What is a Maven repository, and how do local and remote repositories differ?
questions.title: Maven Repositories: Local, Central, and Remote
questions.direct_answer: Maven resolves artifacts through a local repository on the developer machine and configured remote repositories. Maven Central is the default public remote in Maven's standard setup; a company Nexus or Artifactory server is another remote and may proxy Central. Central is not a third repository category—it is one remote repository.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how Maven resolves dependencies — essential for debugging dependency conflicts and build failures
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about the local .m2 cache — this is why dependencies download once and resolve from disk afterward, avoiding repeated downloads
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Nexus and Artifactory as enterprise repository managers and explain why companies use them: security scanning, faster builds, and hosting private internal libraries

sections.title: How Maven Resolves Dependencies
sections.content:
A **Maven repository** stores artifacts and metadata identified by coordinates such as group ID, artifact ID, and version. The **local repository**, normally under `~/.m2/repository`, caches downloaded artifacts and stores artifacts installed by local builds. Maven can also use one or more **remote repositories**.

Maven Central is the standard public remote used by default in ordinary Maven configuration. A company may configure Nexus, Artifactory, or another repository manager as a remote that hosts internal artifacts and optionally proxies public repositories. Security scanning, retention, and proxy behavior are product features and company configuration—not automatic properties of every remote repository.

Maven first consults local state and then follows repository and update policies for missing or changing artifacts. Offline builds work only when every required dependency, plugin, parent, and metadata item is already available locally.

sections.title: Three Repository Tiers
sections.content:
amber|Local|~~/.m2/repository|disk cache on your machine|checked first, instant|reused across projects
blue|Central|~repo.maven.apache.org/maven2|public open-source libs|the default remote|millions of artifacts
emerald|Remote / Nexus|~Company-hosted|proxies Central|hosts private libs|security scanning
violet|Resolution order|~Nearest first|local then remote|download only if missing|deleting ~/.m2 re-fetches

sections.title: Maven Repository Configuration
sections.content:
```xml
<!-- pom.xml - configuring custom remote repository -->
<project>
    <repositories>
        <!-- Company Nexus proxy for faster builds -->
        <repository>
            <id>company-nexus</id>
            <url>https://nexus.company.com/repository/maven-public</url>
        </repository>
    </repositories>
    
    <dependencies>
        <!-- Maven checks: ~/.m2 -> Nexus -> Central -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.company</groupId>
            <artifactId>internal-utils</artifactId>
            <version>2.1.0</version>
        </dependency>
        
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
            <version>3.2.0</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</project>
```

sections.title: When to Configure Repositories
sections.content:
Use the **local repository** automatically — Maven creates it at ~/.m2 on first run and you never configure it manually.

Use **Maven Central** as the default for open-source dependencies — it's preconfigured in Maven and requires no setup. Configure a **remote repository** when your company runs Nexus or Artifactory — add it to settings.xml or pom.xml so Maven pulls dependencies through the company proxy instead of directly from Central. This speeds up builds, enforces security policies, and lets you publish internal libraries. If you're building a library for others to use, publish it to Maven Central (for open-source) or your company Nexus (for internal tools).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Deleting the .m2 directory thinking it's temporary**: Freshers see ~/.m2 taking gigabytes and delete it, then wonder why Maven re-downloads every dependency on the next build. It's a cache that should persist.
- **Not understanding the resolution order**: They don't realize Maven checks local first, so an offline build can work when every dependency, plugin, parent, and required metadata item is already local.
- **Ignoring repository managers in companies**: They hardcode Maven Central URLs instead of using the company Nexus, bypassing security scans and slower builds when Central is slow.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Local repository:** machine-local cache and installed artifacts, usually under `~/.m2/repository`.
- **Remote repository:** network source for artifacts and metadata.
- **Maven Central:** the standard public remote, not a separate repository type.
- **Company manager:** may host private artifacts and proxy approved public sources.
- **Offline limit:** all required dependencies, plugins, parents, and metadata must already be local.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Maven repository stores artifacts and metadata by coordinates. Maven has a local repository on the developer machine and can use one or more remote repositories. Maven Central is the familiar public remote. A company Nexus or Artifactory server is also a remote repository and may proxy Central or host private artifacts.

For example, `mvn install` places the current project's artifact in the local repository so another local build can resolve it. `mvn deploy` publishes to the configured deployment repository when credentials and distribution management are set. Deleting part of `.m2` is sometimes a troubleshooting step, but it removes cached and locally installed artifacts and causes needed items to be resolved or rebuilt again; it is not inherently dangerous or guaranteed to involve a particular download size.

questions.question: What is a build lifecycle in the context of build tools?
questions.title: Build Lifecycle Concept
questions.direct_answer: A build lifecycle is a defined sequence of phases like validate, compile, test, package, install, and deploy. Each phase represents a stage in the build process. Running a later phase automatically executes all prior phases — for example, mvn package runs compile and test first.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how build tools work conceptually before diving into specific Maven commands and plugin configurations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that running mvn package also runs compile and test first — they think each command is independent
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that plugins bind their goals to specific lifecycle phases — this is how Maven's lifecycle model is extensible and how custom tasks integrate

sections.title: Understanding Maven's Build Lifecycle
sections.content:
Maven organizes the build process into a **build lifecycle** — a predefined sequence of **phases** that run in strict order.

Think of it like a manufacturing assembly line where each station must complete before the next begins. Maven has three built-in lifecycles: **default** (compile, test, package, deploy), **clean** (delete build artifacts), and **site** (generate documentation). The default lifecycle has these key phases in order: **validate** (check project structure), **compile** (turn .java into .class), **test** (run JUnit tests), **package** (create JAR/WAR), **verify** (run integration tests), **install** (copy to local ~/.m2), and **deploy** (upload to remote Nexus). The critical insight: when you run **mvn package**, Maven doesn't just package — it runs validate, compile, and test first automatically. Each phase is a container where **plugins** bind their **goals** (tasks). For example, the maven-compiler-plugin binds its compile goal to the compile phase. This design makes Maven extensible — you add plugins to inject custom tasks into the lifecycle without changing core Maven.

sections.title: Default Lifecycle: Each Phase Runs the Ones Before It
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  V[validate] --> C[compile] --> T[test] --> P[package] --> Ve[verify] --> I[install] --> D[deploy]
```

sections.title: Lifecycle Phases in Action
When to Use Each Phase
sections.content:
Use **mvn compile** during active development to quickly check if code compiles without running slow tests.

Use **mvn test** to run unit tests — this is what runs in your IDE's test runner and in CI pull request checks.

Use **mvn package** when you want the final JAR artifact to test locally or deploy manually — this is the minimum phase for a complete build.

Use **mvn install** when building a library that other local projects depend on — it places the JAR in ~/.m2 so dependent projects can find it.

Use **mvn deploy** in CI/CD pipelines to publish releases to company Nexus or Maven Central. Understanding phase dependencies prevents confusion: don't run test separately then package — package already includes test.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking each command is independent**: Freshers run mvn compile, then mvn test, then mvn package, not realizing package already includes compile and test — they're wasting time.
- **Skipping tests incorrectly**: They run mvn package -DskipTests thinking it's the same as mvn package, not understanding it's a flag that breaks the lifecycle contract.
- **Not knowing about plugin bindings**: They don't understand that the maven-surefire-plugin goal runs during the test phase, so configuring plugins requires understanding lifecycle attachment points.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Build Lifecycle**: Predefined sequence of phases that execute in strict order when you invoke a Maven command
- **Phase Dependency**: Running a later phase like package automatically executes earlier phases like compile and test
- **Default Lifecycle**: Primary lifecycle with phases: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy
- **Clean Lifecycle**: Separate lifecycle with a single clean phase that deletes the target directory before building
- **Plugin Goals**: Individual tasks that plugins attach to specific lifecycle phases to perform work like compiling or testing

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A build lifecycle is a sequence of phases that Maven executes in order to build your project. Think of it like steps on an assembly line. Maven has three lifecycles: default for building, clean for deleting old artifacts, and site for generating docs. The default lifecycle has key phases in this order: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, and deploy. Here's the critical part: these phases depend on each other. When you run mvn package, Maven doesn't just create the JAR. It first runs validate to check your pom.xml, then compile to turn Java into bytecode, then test to run JUnit tests, and finally package to bundle everything into a JAR. Each phase is a container where plugins attach their tasks. For example, the maven-compiler-plugin binds to the compile phase and runs javac. The maven-surefire-plugin binds to the test phase and runs your unit tests. This design makes Maven extensible — you can add plugins that hook into lifecycle phases without changing Maven itself. In practice, you run mvn clean install during development, which deletes old builds and puts the new JAR in your local ~/.m2. In CI pipelines, you run mvn deploy to upload artifacts to Nexus. One mistake freshers make is not understanding phase dependencies. They run compile, then test, then package as separate commands, not realizing package already does all three. That wastes time and can cause inconsistencies.
